unit.title: Coordinate and manage basic installation projects

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before your team goes to site to install a steel canopy at a school, which papers should the coordinator have in hand?
options: Only the client's phone number and the site address
A price list from the steel supplier
The welders' pay slips for the month
Approved drawings, the agreed scope and a programme

questions.stem: Which task belongs to the project coordinator rather than to the welders on a canopy job?
options: Booking the crane and agreeing the lift date
Running the root pass on each column joint
Grinding the welds flush before painting
Holding the tag line during the lift

questions.stem: The builder must cast the holding-down bolts into the bases before your columns arrive. What should the coordinator do?
options: Let the builder place them by eye
Wait until the columns arrive, then decide
Give a bolt setting plan and check them before the pour
Plan to drill new holes in the base plates on site later

questions.stem: On a warehouse mezzanine job, the electricians need to fix cable trays to your steel. When should their brackets be agreed?
options: After the steel is painted and fixed
At planning, so cleats can be welded in the shop
Never, because they can drill the steel wherever they like
On handover day, when everyone is on site

questions.stem: Why should the coordinator check that the client has building approval from the local authority before a large steel shed is put up?
options: The approval is what sets the colour that the steel must be
Work without approval may have to be stopped or removed
The welders need it to buy electrodes
It tells the shop which crane to hire

questions.stem: In the programme for a steel canopy, which of these is a milestone?
options: Buying a box of grinding discs
Lunch break on the first day
A welder's day off
Columns erected and plumbed

questions.stem: Your shop has one engine-driven welder, and two site jobs both need it on Tuesday. What should the coordinator do?
options: Re-plan one job's welding or hire a second set
Send it to whichever team asks first
Let both teams share it by moving it at lunch
Tell one team to use the shop's mains set on site

questions.stem: Which team member should the coordinator choose to weld the column splices that the drawing marks as full-strength welds?
options: The newest apprentice, to give him some practice
Whoever is free on that day
A welder qualified for that joint and position
The crane driver, while waiting between lifts

questions.stem: Your team will weld overhead on a canopy above a shop entrance that stays open. What must the coordinator arrange?
options: Barriers, a covered walkway or a closed area below
A sign asking customers to walk quickly
Welding only at moments when no customers are looking up
A helper to catch sparks with a bucket

questions.stem: Before welding starts beside the timber store of a hardware shop, what must be in place?
options: Only the welder's helmet and gloves
A water hose that can reach the timber
A hot work permit, cleared area, extinguisher and fire watch
A phone call to the welder's supervisor at the shop to ask

questions.stem: A fire watch is posted for hot work on a canopy beside a timber store. Why must the fire watch stay on after the welders have packed up?
options: To guard the tools against theft until morning
To count the electrodes used
To sign the welder's timesheet
Smouldering material can catch fire later

questions.stem: A beam to be lifted by crane weighs about 1.8 tonnes. What must the coordinator check about the slings and shackles?
options: That they were all bought new this year
That their SWL is right for the load and rig
That they are the same colour
That they are long enough to reach the crane hook

questions.stem: During a crane lift, who should give the signals to the crane driver?
options: Any worker on site who happens to see the load
The client, as it is her site
One trained signaller agreed in the lift plan
Whoever is standing nearest to the crane

questions.stem: The forecast says strong winds tomorrow, the day of the main lift. What should the coordinator do?
options: Check the crane's wind limit and be ready to postpone
Start very early and lift before the wind gets too strong
Tie extra ropes on the load and carry on
Ask the crane driver to lift faster

questions.stem: The client later claims your team damaged her paving on 12 May. Which record will help most?
options: The shop's price list for that year
The welders' training certificates
The steel supplier's invoice
The site diary with dated photos

questions.stem: The welders think a beam on the drawing is 'too heavy for the job' and want to use a lighter one. Who should approve such a change?
options: The welders, as they know steel
The design engineer, in writing
The crane driver, who lifts it
The client's security guard

questions.stem: After the first week, the crew has erected 6 of 15 columns but has used half of the planned hours. What should the coordinator conclude?
options: The job is running behind and over its labour budget
The job is on time, as half the week has gone
The crew is well ahead and so can take Friday off work
Nothing, as the first week is always slow

questions.stem: The galvaniser phones to say the canopy steel will come back a week later than planned. What is the coordinator's best first step?
options: Wait and say nothing until it arrives
Send the whole crew home without pay for the week
Tell the client and re-plan other work meanwhile
Fit painted steel instead without asking

questions.stem: The site is near the sea in Port Antonio, and the steel will sit on site for two weeks before erection. Which risk should be planned for?
options: The steel getting too hot to lift
Salt and rain damaging the coating
The steel shrinking in the sea air
Birds nesting in the hollow sections

questions.stem: A hired crane company will do the main lift. What should the coordinator get from them before the day?
options: Only their price for the day and the start time
A photo of the crane driver
Their bank account details
Crane test papers and the operator's competence

questions.stem: Before the roof sheets go on a steel shed, the coordinator has the frame checked for plumb, line and bolt tightness. Why at this stage?
options: Faults are easy to fix before the cladding hides them
The roofers will not work on a checked frame
It is cheaper to inspect after the roof is on
The client will not pay a cent until the sheets are on

questions.stem: The drawing says the column base nuts must be tightened to a set torque. How should this be checked?
options: By hand, as tight as the strongest fitter can make it
By eye, if the nut is touching the washer
By hitting each nut with a hammer
With a calibrated torque wrench, and recorded

questions.stem: Which item belongs in the handover pack for a steel canopy?
options: The welders' timesheets
As-built drawings and inspection records
The crane company's price list
The shop's electrode stock record for the month

questions.stem: On the last day, the client points out three rough weld ends and a missing cap on a post. How should these be handled?
options: Ignore them, as the job is now finished
Charge extra to put them right
List them, agree a date and fix them
Tell the client the painters did it

questions.stem: After the job, the crew says the steel came in one load and blocked the site for two days. What should the coordinator do with this?
options: Ignore it, as the job is over and paid
Blame the driver for the delay
Plan staged deliveries on the next job
Ask for a bigger site next time

questions.stem: The budget for a job is J$800 000, with 10% of it kept back as contingency. How much is the contingency?
A beam is 7.5 m long and has a mass of 40 kg per metre. What is its mass?
options: 280 kg
320 kg
340 kg
300 kg

questions.stem: Erection needs 96 labour hours, and the crew works 8-hour days. How many people are needed to finish in 3 days?
options: 3 people
4 people
5 people
6 people

questions.stem: On a busy site, the hired engine-driven welder must run for most of the day. Which spot should the coordinator choose for it?
options: Outdoors, with exhaust away from people and openings
Inside the building, to keep it out of the rain and sun
Next to the fuel store so refuelling is easy
Under the stairs, out of everyone's way

questions.stem: A worker reports a near miss: a loose bolt fell from the steelwork and landed near the client's car. What should the coordinator do?
options: Nothing, as nobody was hurt
Tell the worker to keep quiet about it
Ask the client to park her car further away from now on
Record it, find the cause and put controls in place

questions.stem: Used paint tins and solvent rags are piling up on site. What is the right way to deal with them?
options: Burn them in a drum on site
Store them safely and dispose as the rules say
Leave them for the client to clear
Put them all in the client's household bin when no one sees

questions.stem: Revision A and revision B of the canopy drawing are both pinned up in the site hut. What should the coordinator do?
options: Let each welder choose the one he likes
Keep both up, as they are nearly the same
Use B, and mark A superseded or remove it
Use A, since it was issued first

questions.stem: A worker falls from a ladder on site and cannot move. What should the coordinator do first?
options: Make the area safe, call for help and give first aid
Lift him into a car and drive him straight to hospital
Finish the lift, then deal with him
Ask him to try standing up

questions.stem: Your team must weld brackets 5 m up on a warehouse wall. Which access is best?
options: A ladder leaned on the wall
Standing on a stack of pallets
Climbing the existing racking
A MEWP or a proper scaffold

questions.stem: The client's manager wants to know when the main entrance will be closed for the lift. When should you tell her?
options: On the morning of the lift, when the crane arrives
After the lift is finished
Well in advance, with the date, time and route
Only if she asks you again

questions.stem: A welder on the crew does not hold the qualification for the overhead welds on the canopy. How should the coordinator use him?
options: Let him do the overhead welds anyway
Give him work he is qualified for
Send him home for the week
Let him weld if no one is watching

questions.stem: Why should the coordinator check the inspection tag on the hired scaffold before the welders use it?
options: It shows it was inspected and is safe to use
It shows the scaffold has been paid for
It tells you who owns each of the boards and clips
It tells the welders when to have lunch

questions.stem: Fabricated parts arrive on site with no piece marks on them. What problem will this cause?
options: The steel will rust faster
The crane is not allowed to lift unmarked steel
The client will not pay for them
Parts may be fitted in the wrong place

questions.stem: Why should the coordinator walk round the finished canopy with the client before signing off?
options: To show off the welds to her friends and neighbours
So any snags are found and agreed together
To collect cash for the final payment
To ask her to sweep the site

questions.stem: The site is next to houses in Portmore. Which plan helps keep good relations with the neighbours?
options: Work late at night when it is cooler
Grind only at weekends, when most of them are at home
Agree working hours and screen sparks and noise
Burn offcuts and packing in the yard

questions.stem: Where should the oxy-acetylene cylinders be kept on site overnight?
options: Upright, chained, in a ventilated, locked store
Lying flat on the floor at the back of the site hut
Beside the generator so they stay warm
In the client's basement, out of sight

questions.stem: A frame has 24 connections to weld on site, and 18 are done. What percentage of the welding is complete?
Which test is best suited to checking the site column splice welds for surface cracks?
options: A bend test cut from the column
Tapping with a hammer
A water pressure test
Dye penetrant or magnetic particle

questions.stem: The engineer must pass the bolted connections before the roof frame goes on. Why should this inspection appear as a task in the programme?
options: So the crew can have a rest day
Work above cannot go on until it is passed
So the engineer can charge for more of his hours
So the client has time to choose paint

questions.stem: Which item is most needed when planning the site layout for a steelwork job?
options: Where the crane, deliveries and storage will go
Where each of the welders will park his own car
Where the client keeps her office files
Where the nearest hardware store is

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Before your crew erects the canopy, the client asks for the paper that lists each step of the erection, its hazards and how each is controlled. What is this paper usually called?
A mobile crane is hired at J$18 000 an hour, with a 4-hour minimum charge. The lift takes 2.5 hours. What is the hire charge, in J$?
What is the written plan called that sets out the load, the crane, the slings, the lifting area and the people for a crane lift?
What are the bolts called that are cast into a concrete base to fix a steel column's base plate?
Hot work ends at 3 p.m., but a trained person stays until 4 p.m. checking for smouldering material. What is this person's role called?
Painting the handrails can start any time in a 4-day window without delaying the canopy's finish date. What is this spare time on the programme called?
What is the name for a stage in a job past which work must not go until an inspection has been done and signed?
The steel erection budget was J$500 000. The final cost is J$575 000. What percentage overspend is this?
Scissor lifts and boom lifts used for welding at height are known by a four-letter short name. What do those four letters stand for?
A shackle is stamped '2 t SWL'. In words, what does SWL mean?
One purlin is 5.4 m long and has a mass of 6 kg per metre. The roof has 10 purlins. What is their total mass, in kg?
A frame has 12 base plates with 4 holding-down bolts each. The coordinator orders 10% extra, rounded up to whole bolts. How many bolts are ordered?
Erection starts on Monday 9 November 2026 and needs 8 working days (Monday to Friday, no public holidays). On what date should it finish?
At the close-out meeting, the crew lists what they would do differently next time. In two words, what are these points called?
Which permit must be issued before welding or cutting is done on an occupied site where things that can burn are nearby?

essays.stem: You are coordinating the supply and installation of a steel canopy over the entrance of a school in May Pen. Describe how you would set up the project before any steel goes to site.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check that I have the approved drawings, the agreed scope and price, and any building approval, and I would visit the site with the school to agree access, working hours and how pupils will be kept away. I would write a programme with milestones: bases ready, steel delivered, columns up, roof frame fixed, sheeting, painting touch-up and handover. I would list the resources: a qualified welding crew, an engine-driven welder, a crane or hoist, a scaffold or MEWP, and the bolts and consumables. I would book the crane early and get its test papers. I would write a risk assessment and method statement, a lift plan and a hot work plan with a fire watch, and arrange barriers and signs. I would agree with the builder the bolt setting plan for the bases. Finally I would hold a start-up meeting with the crew and the school to go through the plan, roles and contacts.
markingPoints: Checks drawings, scope, price and approvals; visits the site
Programme with clear milestones
Resources listed and booked (crew, plant, crane, access)
Safety documents: risk assessment, method statement, lift plan, hot work and fire watch, barriers
Coordinates bases with the builder and holds a start-up meeting

essays.stem: Explain how you would coordinate your erection team with the masons, the roofers, the electricians and the painters on a steel mezzanine job in a warehouse.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by agreeing the order of work with the main contractor and every trade. The masons must cast the bases and holding-down bolts first, to our bolt setting plan, and I would check the bolts before the concrete is poured and again before we erect. Next my team erects and bolts or welds the frame, and the engineer inspects it. The electricians need cleats for cable trays and lights, so I would get their positions at planning and have the cleats welded in the shop, to avoid drilling or welding on site later. The flooring or roof team follows once the frame is passed. The painters touch up last, after all site welding is done. I would put all of this on one programme, hold a short weekly coordination meeting, and send any changes in writing. Hot work would be planned so that no other trade is working below or near flammable materials at the time.
markingPoints: Agrees the order of work with all trades
Bases and bolts checked before the pour and before erection
Other trades' fixings agreed at planning and made in the shop
One programme, regular coordination meetings, changes in writing
Hot work planned so other trades are not exposed

essays.stem: A 2-tonne steel beam must be lifted onto columns by a hired mobile crane. Explain how you would plan and control the lift.
essays.modelAnswer: I would have a written lift plan prepared and approved by a competent person. It would state the mass of the beam, the crane's capacity at the radius needed, the slings and shackles with their safe working loads, and the lifting points. I would check that the crane and its operator are certified and competent, and that the ground can take the crane's outriggers, with mats where needed. I would check for overhead power lines and keep well clear of them. On the day I would set up an exclusion zone with barriers so no one stands under the load, and appoint one trained signaller. Tag lines would be used to steady the beam. Before lifting, I would brief the whole crew on the plan and their roles, and check the weather against the crane's wind limit. The beam would be lifted a little first to check balance, then placed and secured before the slings are released.
markingPoints: Written lift plan by a competent person: mass, capacity, radius, slings and SWL
Crane and operator certified; ground and overhead lines checked
Exclusion zone, one trained signaller and tag lines
Crew briefing and weather or wind check
Trial lift, then place and secure before releasing slings

essays.stem: Explain how you would control hot work on a site where the client's business stays open while your team welds new handrails.
essays.modelAnswer: I would agree with the client which areas and times we can work, and plan the noisiest and most spark-producing work for quiet periods. Before any welding, a hot work permit would be issued for each area and day. The area would be checked and cleared of anything that can burn, and what cannot be moved would be covered with fire blankets. I would screen the welding so the public cannot see the arc, and put up barriers and signs so customers and staff are kept away. A trained fire watch would stand by with a suitable extinguisher during the work and for the set time after it, as the permit says. I would check that the engine-driven welder is outside, with its fumes away from doors and windows, and that leads do not cross walkways. At the end of each day, the area would be checked again and the permit closed and signed.
markingPoints: Agrees areas and times with the client
Hot work permit for each area and day
Area cleared or covered; screens, barriers and signs for the public
Fire watch with extinguisher during and after the work
Fumes and leads controlled; final check and permit closed

essays.stem: Your four-week steelwork job is one week in, and you suspect it is slipping. Describe how you would measure progress and cost against the plan, and what you would do to bring it back.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set a baseline at the start: the programme, the planned labour hours for each stage and the budget for materials, plant and labour. Each day I would record in the site diary what was done, hours worked, deliveries, plant used and any delays. Each week I would compare the work done with the plan, for example columns erected or connections welded, and the hours and money spent with the budget. If 40% of the work is done but 50% of the hours are used, the job is behind and over on labour. I would find the cause, such as late steel, rain, a missing crane or rework. Then I would act: re-order the tasks so the crew can keep working, add a welder or extra hours if the budget allows, chase the supplier, or agree a new date with the client. I would report progress to my manager and the client every week, honestly, with the action I am taking.
markingPoints: Baseline: programme, planned hours and budget
Daily records in the site diary
Weekly comparison of work done and money spent against plan
Finds the cause of any delay and takes corrective action
Reports honestly to the manager and the client

essays.stem: When your columns arrive on site, you find that the holding-down bolts cast by the builder are 30 mm out of position. Explain what you would do and why.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stop the erection of those columns and not force them on or cut the bolts. I would measure and record every bolt position against the drawing and take photos, so the problem is clear. Then I would tell the main contractor and the client in writing, and ask the design engineer for a solution, because only the engineer can decide how the connection can be safely changed. Possible solutions include slotting or re-drilling the base plates, new bolts set with an approved resin anchor, or a new base plate, but the welders must not choose one alone. While waiting, I would re-plan the crew onto other work, such as columns whose bolts are correct. Once the engineer's instruction is in writing, we would carry it out and have it inspected. I would record the extra time and cost as a variation, because the fault was not ours, and note the lesson: check bolts before the pour next time.
markingPoints: Stops erection; does not force, bend or cut bolts
Measures, records and photographs the problem
Informs contractor and client in writing; asks the engineer for the solution
Re-plans the crew meanwhile; carries out the approved fix and has it inspected
Records the time and cost as a variation and the lesson learned

essays.stem: Describe the inspections and checks you would plan at stages during the installation of a steel frame, and say why each matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Before erection I would check the bases and holding-down bolts for position, level and projection, because a fault here throws out the whole frame. When the steel arrives, I would check piece marks, sizes, coating and damage against the delivery note, so the right parts go in the right places. After the columns are up, I would check them for plumb and line before the beams are fitted, while it is still easy to adjust. After bolting, I would check the bolt grade, washers and tightening, with a calibrated torque wrench where the drawing gives a value. Site welds would be checked visually by the welder and the inspector, with dye penetrant or magnetic particle testing where the drawing asks. Finally, touch-up painting would be checked for coverage and thickness. Each check would be a hold point, recorded and signed before the next stage starts, so faults are found early and the client has proof of quality.
markingPoints: Bases and bolts checked before erection
Delivered steel checked against the delivery note and drawings
Plumb and line checked before beams are fixed
Bolts and site welds checked (torque, visual, NDT where required)
Hold points recorded and signed; says why early checks matter

essays.stem: The steel frame for a warehouse mezzanine is finished. Describe the handover to the client step by step, and list the records you would give her, saying why each one matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Before handover, my team would finish all work, clear the site of offcuts, rod stubs, packing and waste, and do a final inspection against the drawings. Then I would walk round with the client and list any snags, with a date to fix each. Once they are cleared, she signs the handover form. I would explain care and limits: keep the floor within the load the engineer designed it for, check and touch up the paint each year, and never cut, drill or weld the frame without asking the engineer. The records would be: as-built drawings, so anyone changing the mezzanine later knows exactly what is there; inspection and test records for welds and bolts, which prove the work met the standard; material certificates where the job needs them, to show the steel grade; the paint data, so touch-ups use the right system; and the warranty and our contacts, so she knows who to call. I would keep copies in the job file.
markingPoints: Work finished, site cleared and final inspection done
Walk-round with the client; snag list cleared and handover signed
Explains care and limits (design load, no cutting or welding without advice)
Lists the records: as-built drawings, inspection and test records, certificates, paint data, warranty
Says why each record matters; keeps copies

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan the delivery, storage and protection of fabricated steelwork on a tight town-centre site in Montego Bay.
essays.modelAnswer: On a tight site there is little room, so I would plan deliveries in stages, in the order the steel will be erected, rather than all at once. I would agree delivery times with the client and the police or the local authority if the road must be used, avoiding busy hours. I would plan where the truck parks, where the crane or forklift unloads and where each load is laid down. Steel would be stored off the ground on timber bearers, with drainage, and clearly piece-marked so it can be found. Painted or galvanised steel would be protected from damage by slings, using soft slings or packing, and covered if it must wait, because the sea air in Montego Bay quickly attacks bare or damaged steel. Bolts and consumables would go in a locked store. Each delivery would be checked against the delivery note, and any damage recorded and reported.
markingPoints: Staged deliveries in erection order
Agreed delivery times, road use and unloading area
Stored off the ground, drained and piece-marked
Coatings protected from slings and sea air; small items locked away
Each delivery checked and damage recorded

essays.stem: Your canopy project finished a week late and J$60 000 over budget. Explain how you would review what happened and make sure the next project goes better.
essays.modelAnswer: I would gather the facts first: the programme against the actual dates, the budget against the real costs, the site diary, the variations and any incident reports. Then I would hold a short review meeting with the crew and, if possible, the client. We would look at what went well and what went wrong, and find the causes without blaming people. For example, the week's delay might have come from the galvaniser returning steel late and from rework on bases that were out of position; the extra cost might be crane standing time and overtime. For each cause we would agree an action, such as booking galvanising earlier with a buffer, checking holding-down bolts before the pour, and confirming the crane only once the bases are passed. I would write these up as lessons learned, share them with the office, and build them into the planning checklist and price for the next job.
markingPoints: Gathers facts: plan versus actual time and cost, diary, variations
Holds a review with the crew (and client) without blame
Finds the real causes of delay and overspend
Agrees specific actions for each cause
Records lessons learned and builds them into the next plan

practical1.title: Plan the installation of a steel canopy: programme, resources, method statement and start-up meeting
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a drawing pack and a site brief for a steel canopy over a building entrance (columns on new bases, beams, purlins and sheeting). As the project team, produce a project plan and run a start-up meeting. Share the roles: coordinator (programme as a Gantt chart with milestones), safety lead (risk assessment and method statement, including hot work with a fire watch and work at height), lifting lead (outline lift plan with masses worked out from the section sizes given), materials lead (delivery and storage plan and a bolt list with spares) and quality lead (inspection and hold-point plan). In a group of four, the coordinator also takes the quality role. Each member writes and signs their own part. Then run a 15-minute start-up meeting with the assessor playing the client: each member presents their part, the client raises two problems and the group agrees actions. One member takes minutes. Photograph each part.
materials: Drawing pack and site brief from the assessor, with section masses given
Gantt chart, risk assessment, method statement, lift plan and inspection plan templates
Squared paper, rulers, calculators and coloured pens
Flip chart or whiteboard for the start-up meeting
photos: The group reading the drawing pack, with roles written up
The finished Gantt chart with milestones marked
The risk assessment and method statement, signed
The lift plan with the masses worked out
The delivery plan, bolt list and inspection plan
The signed minutes with actions and owners
checklist: Read the drawings and brief correctly and used the right sizes and quantities
Produced their part of the plan clearly, complete and signed
Worked out masses, quantities or durations correctly
Included hot work control, fire watch, work at height and lifting controls where they apply
Linked their part to the others (for example lift dates on the programme, hold points before the next stage)
Presented their part clearly at the start-up meeting and answered the client's questions
Helped agree actions, owners and dates for the problems raised
safety: Treat the plan as real: every hazard named must have a control
Keep to the Centre's rules on hot work, lifting and work at height when writing the method statement
Speak respectfully in the meeting; let each member present without interruption
Keep the classroom tidy and clear of trip hazards

practical2.title: Coordinate a staged installation of a small steel frame at the Centre, with hold-point checks and handover
practical2.brief: The assessor provides a small pre-made steel frame or stand (for example a bolted tank stand or a handrail section) to be installed on a base or training bay at the Centre, and its drawing. Your group plans and carries out the installation in stages, with one member acting as coordinator for each stage: (1) set out and check the base or fixing points against the drawing, (2) receive and check the parts, (3) position and bolt the frame, then check plumb, level and line, (4) weld the fixing brackets or cleats shown on the drawing, under a hot work permit with a fire watch, (5) final inspection, snag list, clean-up and handover to the assessor as client. Each stage coordinator briefs the group, fills in the site diary and the hold-point sheet, and signs the stage off only when it passes. Every member takes part in the physical work and coordinates at least one stage. Hand over a short pack: the diary, the hold-point sheets, the snag list and a marked-up as-built sketch.
materials: Small steel frame or stand in parts, its drawing, bolts, nuts and washers (from the assessor)
Base, training bay or fixing plate at the Centre
Measuring tape, spirit level, square and string line
Spanners and a torque wrench if the drawing gives a torque
MMAW or MIG set for the brackets, with full welding PPE, screens and a fire extinguisher
Hot work permit, site diary, hold-point sheets, snag list and handover templates
photos: The base or fixing points measured and checked against the drawing
The parts laid out and checked against the parts list
The frame bolted in place, with the level on it
Welding the brackets behind screens, with the fire watch in place
The signed hold-point sheets and site diary
The finished frame, cleaned up, during the handover walk-round
checklist: As stage coordinator, briefed the group clearly on the task, hazards and roles
Checked work against the drawing and recorded measurements accurately
Did not let work pass a hold point until it was checked and signed
Took part safely in lifting, bolting and positioning (team lifts, correct tools)
